title: Va'era: why Aaron struck the river (Exodus 7:19)
hookLine: Rashi: Moses didn't strike the Nile because it once saved his life

cards: People get attached to strange things. The old car that got you through college. The bench in the hospital garden where you waited for news.
The tree you climbed as a kid. You'd feel something if someone took a chainsaw to it, even though it's just wood, just metal. For Moses, the Nile isn't just a river.

When he was three months old, his mother put him in a little basket, sealed it with pitch, and set it among the reeds. That water carried him to safety. And now God is about to turn the Nile to blood.

teach.h: SAY UNTO AARON: TAKE THY ROD.
teach.b: Here's the detail. For the first plague, God doesn't tell Moses to strike the water. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Say unto Aaron: Take thy rod, and stretch out thy hand over the waters of Egypt."
Aaron, not Moses. Why the switch? Moses is the one who spoke with God at the bush, and Moses carries the staff.
Rashi, passing on an older midrash, gives the answer: the river protected Moses when he was thrown into it as a baby, so it wasn't right for him to be the one to strike it.
The second plague, the frogs, comes up out of the river: Aaron again. The third, the lice, comes from striking the dust of the ground: Aaron again. Rashi says the dust protected Moses too.
When he killed the Egyptian taskmaster, he hid the body in the sand.
The earth kept his secret, so it, too, was spared his hand. It's an odd idea. A river doesn't know it saved anyone, and sand doesn't have feelings.
The point isn't what the water feels. It's what Moses becomes if he can strike, without a second thought, the thing that saved him.
The Talmud has a saying for this: a well you drank from, don't throw a clod of earth into it.
Jewish tradition calls the trait hakarat hatov, recognizing the good.
Not just saying thanks, but remembering, long after, who and what carried you.

how: Hakarat hatov, recognizing the good, is taught as a Jewish value; the Modeh Ani said on waking thanks God for returning the soul, and traditional blessings are said over food, water and ordinary moments.

o: and I appeared, the portion where the plagues begin
the blood, the first plague on the waters of Egypt
and he struck, Aaron's rod over the river Nile

games.q: who struck what, and why — tap the pairs.
p: struck the river and the dust

s: Moses struck the Nile to start the first plague
God told Moses to tell Aaron to stretch out his rod over the waters.
Rashi explains Aaron struck the dust because it once protected Moses
Moses hid the Egyptian he killed in the sand.
the Talmud says don't throw a clod into a well you drank from
Bava Kamma 92b cites it as a popular proverb about not scorning what served you.

games.q: you're Moses. God is about to turn the Nile to blood, the river that carried you as a baby. who strikes it?
o: no one; it turns by itself.
games.why: God told Moses: say unto Aaron, take thy rod. Rashi says the river had protected Moses, so it wasn't fitting for him to strike it.

practice: Think of something, not someone, that carried you through: a car that got you to the hospital in time, the library where you hid from a hard home, a song, a city, a bed, a coat.
Picture it and thank it silently, even though it can't hear. Then ask yourself whether there's anything like it you've been treating carelessly lately.

wordCard.voice: Va'era. The portion of the first plagues, where Aaron strikes the Nile because, Rashi says, the river once saved Moses.

orig.note: Hebrew: recognizing the good. The Jewish name for gratitude that remembers.

carryVoice: Your line: gratitude even to water. Before it ever turned to blood, the river carried him. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Say unto Aaron: Take thy rod, and stretch out thy hand over the waters of Egypt
